Good video RE: Internet : The US 1st Amendment protected it up until now. Why are we not more upset about this? What stops someone in the UN to just not allowing access to a site?

Though we, as a people, never understood the power and opportunity we had to organize and fight the powers that be and the status quo via the internet, are we not now just fucked? Is the internet just so enigmatic to people that we don't understand the ramifications or do we really just feel that lost and powerless?

The same thing that stops the UN from accomplishing just about anything today - diverse representation. For instance the US tried multiple times to get the UN to take action against Syria. Russia vetoed it every single time. Many nations have tried to get the UN to take action against Israel. The US vetoes it every single time. And so on.

It's the way our government is supposed to work - checks and balances. As recently as 2010 our government was fighting for the right to be able to, at the president's sole discretion, shut down any or all parts of the internet indefinitely. It was in the Protecting Cyberspace as a National Asset Act. The United States is also one of only two western nations listed as enemies of the internet - the other being the UK. All things considered, this hand-off is a great thing. This handoff is likely a great thing for the future of the internet.

When you have centralized control over something it means you need to corrupt one body to screw everything. So for instance one time the US used their ability to block domains on a worldwide scale was with fulltiltpoker.com. They were engaged in the evil and unbelievably heinous crime of allowing US adults to play online poker. The crackdown on online poker was heavily lobbied for by domestic casinos, and individuals like Sheldon Adelson, who felt it was cutting into their business. A multi-nation commission which also has academic and business interests is a much tougher nut to crack. I do wish there was more transparency on the exact power mechanisms in play (will decisions be based on majority vote, are there veto systems?, etc) but in general this is almost certainly going to be an improvement over a single nation that's been headed towards authoritarianism matched with corporate corruption being in 100% control of this aspect of the internet - even if that nation might not feel so bad since we've called it home since before we could walk.
